item.title: Interview: Botswana aims to strengthen, deepen ties with China, says Botswanan president
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
Botswanan President Duma Gideon Boko speaks at an exclusive interview with Xinhua in Gaborone, Botswana, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Wei)
by Xinhua writers Guo Chunju, Xu Jiatong
GABORONE, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Botswana-China relationship is "deep and strong," and Botswana looks forward to deepening bilateral cooperation in trade, the digital economy, renewable energy and other fields, Botswanan President Duma Gideon Boko has said.
In an interview with Xinhua ahead of his first state visit to China since taking office, Boko said that the two sides have maintained "very good, very strong, (and) mutually beneficial diplomatic relationship" for many years.
"China has, over those years, provided immense development assistance to the Republic of Botswana," he said, noting that Botswana looks forward to benefiting from Chinese expertise, including that of companies already operating in Botswana.
"We look forward to broadening and deepening that presence, and inviting others that will participate in mega projects in Botswana," he said.
Botswana is also looking to deepen the trade relationship with China in other ways, including partnering with Chinese companies which "have done massive investment in research and development in relation to beneficiation," Boko said, adding that it would "enable Botswana to become a manufacturer and, therefore, serve the Chinese market even better."
From May 1 this year, China extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties. Regarding the measure as "a very welcome and laudable step by the Chinese government," Boko said that it has opened up "what is a 1.4 billion market in terms of consumer base to African products."
"It makes the trade relations between Africa and China seamless, and will help our economies," he said. "But more importantly, with regard to Botswana, we will be concluding agreements that will enable our citrus produce to enter China under the no-tariff arrangement, which is massive as a benefit to our country."
On digitalization and economic diversification, Boko said that Botswana looks forward to benefiting from the Chinese expertise. "China has the ability, the strength, and the capability ... to deploy those capabilities in Botswana for the benefit of the economy of Botswana, and the broader economy of the SADC (Southern African Development Community) region and the African continent," he said.
The Botswanan president also said that China's development experience in renewable energy, energy storage, power infrastructure and other green industries is exactly what Botswana needs, adding that his country is open to Chinese businesses.
"We are looking forward to meeting those companies, (and) giving them facts about the country and the opportunities, so that they can then choose to deploy their expertise and technologies in the country," he said.
"We certainly look forward to working with China in these regards, and it basically is a matter of building upon a foundation, a very firm and strong foundation that already exists," he added.

item.title: Britain doesn't support Trump's Russia diesel deal: defense secretary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
Photo taken on Oct. 11, 2026 shows Britain's Ministry of Defense in London, Britain. Britain does not support U.S. President Donald Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to purchase millions of tons of diesel from Russia, British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said on Sunday. (Xinhua/Zhang Feng)
LONDON, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Britain does not support U.S. President Donald Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to purchase millions of tons of diesel from Russia, British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said on Sunday.
"We don't support that decision. As the prime minister set out, we are strengthening sanctions against Russia," Streeting said in an interview broadcast by the BBC.
He added that the deal was done "very much in the context of the U.S. midterm elections" in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.
Trump's diesel agreement is aimed at lowering fuel prices in the United States that have risen following the joint U.S.-Israel attacks against Iran, according to the BBC report.
On Friday, Washington announced measures to ease sanctions on Russian diesel trade. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized the move, saying that allowing Russia to sell petroleum products would amount to investing in the war.

item.title: Transatlantic divides over security, development, climate emerge at Arctic assembly
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
Photo taken on Dec. 21, 2016 shows Santa's Igloos Arctic Circle, a glass shelter hotel, in Santa Claus Village, Rovaniemi, Finland. Some say the most romantic way to see the aurora is to lie down in an igloo, a shelter made of glass that allows you to gaze at the lights with ease and comfort. (Xinhua/Li Jizhi)
Discussions revealed contrasting approaches to the region's future, with Washington emphasizing military capabilities and resource development while its allies placed greater weight on sovereignty, local interests and environmental protection.
By Xinhua writers Zhu Haochen, Zhang Yuliang and Zhang Zhaoji
REYKJAVIK, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- The United States and its European and Canadian allies displayed diverging priorities on Arctic security, resource development and climate policy at the 2026 Arctic Circle Assembly, highlighting growing strains in transatlantic relations
As the three-day gathering concluded Saturday in Reykjavik, Iceland, discussions revealed contrasting approaches to the region's future, with Washington emphasizing military capabilities and resource development while its allies placed greater weight on sovereignty, local interests and environmental protection.
HOW TO ENSURE SECURITY?
Founded in 2013 by then-Icelandic President Olafur Ragnar Grimsson, the Arctic Circle holds its annual assembly in Iceland every October and serves as a major international platform for dialogue on Arctic affairs.
Security featured prominently at this year's gathering, but Washington and its allies differed in their priorities. While U.S. officials insisted on expanding military capabilities and infrastructure, European and Canadian officials emphasized sovereignty and autonomy as their paramount concerns.
At Thursday's opening ceremony, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy said the United States was investing billions of dollars to strengthen its military presence in the state. He also outlined plans to work with allies on Arctic ports, airports and shipping networks that could serve military needs.
This photo taken on Jan. 3, 2026 shows a bridge shrouded in icy mist over the Kemijoki River in Rovaniemi, Finland. Rovaniemi, a city located on the Arctic Circle, is renowned worldwide for aurora watching, winter sports, and reindeer sleigh rides. It is also well known internationally as the "home of Santa Claus," attracting large numbers of visitors from around the globe. (Xinhua/Zhu Haochen)
For some U.S. allies, however, concerns over Washington's respect for their sovereignty have complicated security cooperation.
Since returning to the White House in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his intention to take control of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark. Despite a new security agreement reached by the United States, Denmark and Greenland in September, trust among the allies has yet to recover.
In Reykjavik, Greenland's Foreign Minister Mute Egede said Greenlanders had endured enormous pressure and uncertainty, reinforcing the importance of autonomy in determining their future. "We will not be spectators to our own future," he stressed.
U.S.-Canada relations have also deteriorated due to Trump's threats to make Canada the "51st state" and his sharp tariff increases on Canadian goods.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand stressed that the Arctic was not merely a strategic frontier, but also "home" to local people. She said Canada was strengthening "middle-power diplomacy" with Nordic countries and other partners to safeguard peace, security and respect for sovereignty in the Arctic.
Zhao Long, director of the Center for Marine and Polar Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told Xinhua that Arctic affairs were increasingly being securitized amid growing geopolitical rivalry.
He said Washington and its allies did not entirely share the same perceptions of external security threats, making it increasingly difficult for the United States to coordinate a common position amid new tensions among them.
Photo taken on Feb. 2, 2021 shows the aurora Borealis or Northern Lights seen from a tree hotel, located about 150 km south of the Arctic Circle, northern Sweden. (Photo by Wei Xuechao/Xinhua)
HOW TO SHARE DEVELOPMENT BENEFITS?
As global warming opens up the Arctic and makes shipping routes and natural resources increasingly accessible, questions over how to develop the region and distribute the economic benefits have gained prominence.
At the assembly, U.S. officials enthusiastically promoted plans to expand energy development and infrastructure construction, emphasizing the Arctic's strategic and economic value, while Washington's allies placed greater weight on local communities' right to shape development and share in its benefits.
Dunleavy said the Trump administration has been seeking to transform Alaska's development model to support both defense needs and resource exploitation. Thomas Dans, chairman of the U.S. Arctic Research Commission, described U.S. investment in the region as "unprecedented."
Meanwhile, representatives from Greenland, the European Union (EU) and Canada emphasized that Arctic communities should make their own development choices.
"The future of the Arctic cannot be shaped solely by what the world wants to get from the Arctic. It must also take into account what Arctic peoples themselves want," Egede said.
He stressed that development must create opportunities for local residents rather than allow external investment and security infrastructure to override their choices.
Anand also highlighted the Arctic's enormous potential in critical minerals, energy and transportation, but stressed that the key was to ensure that "local people benefit."
This photo taken on Jan. 3, 2026 shows a stall selling coffee and snacks in Rovaniemi, Finland. Rovaniemi, a city located on the Arctic Circle, is renowned worldwide for aurora watching, winter sports, and reindeer sleigh rides. It is also well known internationally as the "home of Santa Claus," attracting large numbers of visitors from around the globe. (Xinhua/Zhu Haochen)
HOW TO TACKLE CLIMATE CHANGE?
Climate change emerged as another major point of divergence between Washington and its allies at the assembly.
European and Canadian representatives prioritized climate action and environmental governance, warning that rising temperatures, thawing permafrost and changes in marine ecosystems were already threatening the region.
Asked whether climate change or military threats concerned him more, Egede chose climate change, saying it was "changing the way local people live."
Anand warned that declining sea ice and thawing permafrost were affecting Arctic ecosystems, food security and local livelihoods. She said climate governance should stand alongside military security and economic development as one of the three major issues facing the Arctic.
European Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela said tackling climate change would remain a central pillar of the EU's Arctic strategy, with environmental protection integrated into every Arctic-related policy.
By contrast, U.S. officials placed less emphasis on climate issues. Dunleavy acknowledged that his discussions with the White House had focused mainly on energy, defense and infrastructure, while climate issues had received "relatively less" attention.
Trump has long dismissed global warming as a "hoax" and announced U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement during both of his presidential terms.
Zhao said Trump's decision to withdraw from the agreement in 2025 had further widened climate policy differences between Washington and its European allies. He warned that downgrading climate cooperation would continue to undermine multilateral governance and scientific cooperation in the Arctic.
Finnish Arctic affairs expert Lassi Heininen said environmental cooperation played an important role in easing military tensions and maintaining geopolitical stability in the region.
He emphasized the importance of preserving such cooperation amid growing strategic competition in the region.

item.title: Xi leads efforts toward building Healthy China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- On a small island in the Yangtze River in eastern China, residents don't need to leave the island to see a medical specialist. They can now access modern medical equipment at the township clinic and consult specialists from higher-level hospitals, who pay regular visits to the facility.
In December 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the clinic in Shiye Township, Jiangsu Province, outlining a path for advancing rural healthcare. Shiye is home to five villages and more than 10,000 permanent residents.
"We must shift the focus of healthcare to the community level, channel more medical resources to local communities, and promote equal access to basic public services in urban and rural areas," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission.
This is to provide people with safe, effective, accessible and affordable public health services and basic medical care, and effectively address the difficulties and high costs people face in accessing medical care at the local level, he added.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in late 2012, the Party Central Committee, with Xi at the core, has given strategic priority to ensuring people's health. It made the major decision to advance the Healthy China Initiative nationwide.
From targeted advances in key areas to nationwide coverage of inclusive health services that meet basic needs, China, a country of more than 1.4 billion people, has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development.
HEALTHCARE FOR ALL
Over the years, Xi has visited grassroots medical institutions and households in rural areas across the country, offering targeted guidance tailored to local conditions.
He has focused on preventing people from falling into or returning to poverty because of illness, using remote consultations to help balance medical resources, and addressing healthcare-related issues in rural areas.
Xi has paid close attention to the issues people face in accessing healthcare at the grassroots level and set out clear directions, from establishing five basic systems -- tiered diagnosis and treatment, modern hospital management, universal medical insurance, drug supply security, and comprehensive oversight -- to developing the healthcare workforce and digital infrastructure for smart healthcare.
"We must unswervingly uphold the public welfare nature of the medical and healthcare sector, and not take the path of wholesale marketization and commercialization," Xi said.
He has also called for further deepening the reform of medical and healthcare systems and exploring Chinese solutions to the worldwide challenge of healthcare reform.
Coordinated development and governance of healthcare services, medical insurance and pharmaceuticals have helped reduce out-of-pocket payments to 27.1 percent of total health expenditure.
The vision of ensuring that serious illnesses can be treated within one's province, common illnesses within one's city or county, and everyday ailments at the grassroots level is increasingly becoming a reality.
China has supported the development of 125 national regional medical centers so far, with 75 percent of their hospitals located in central and western regions and other areas where high-quality medical resources are relatively scarce.
More than 90 percent of residents can access nearby medical and healthcare services within 15 minutes. Primary-level medical institutions account for more than 50 percent of all medical visits nationwide.
COMPREHENSIVE LIFECYCLE HEALTH
Xi has also expressed deep concern over the growing prevalence of myopia among students, particularly at younger ages.
The trend, he has said, seriously affects children's health and poses a major issue for the future of the country, and it must be given high priority and not allowed to continue unchecked.
With strengthened efforts to prevent and control myopia among children and adolescents, China's overall student myopia rate declined for five consecutive years from 2021 to 2025, reaching 49.9 percent in 2025, down 3.7 percentage points from 2018.
From enabling older people to enjoy their later years to preventing childhood obesity and myopia, Xi has stressed the importance of safeguarding health across all population groups and throughout the entire lifecycle.
A range of health indicators point to improvements in the country's overall health status.
In 2025, China's average life expectancy rose to 79.25 years, while its major health indicators remained at the leading position among upper-middle-income countries and countries with a population exceeding 100 million. The premature mortality rate from major chronic diseases fell to 13.8 percent, and major infectious diseases and endemic diseases were brought under effective control.
China aims to establish a health system by 2035 that is compatible with a society that has basically achieved modernization.
Xi has emphasized the translation of scientific and technological innovations into practical applications, called for advancing the digital and intelligent development of healthcare nationwide, and encouraged regions with suitable conditions to explore the application of artificial intelligence.
This year, the government work report included biomedicine as an emerging pillar industry for the first time.
In the first half of 2026 alone, China approved 38 innovative drugs for market entry.
China is developing a growing range of homegrown drugs, medical equipment, vaccines, medical consumables and approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
Traditional Chinese medicine is a distinctive component of China's healthcare system. Xi has issued important instructions on multiple occasions, calling for the sector's industrial development and modernization, as well as wider international reach.
China has also continued to deepen health cooperation with countries around the world by promoting the use of artemisinin to benefit patients worldwide, regularly deploying medical teams abroad, establishing overseas traditional Chinese medicine centers, and joining efforts to combat Ebola. Through these efforts, it has worked with other countries to address cross-border public health risks.
Yet as China's economy and society evolve and its demographic landscape changes, people's healthcare needs are becoming increasingly multi-layered and diverse.
"At present and for a period to come, China's health and healthcare work needs to adapt to changing circumstances and refine certain specific policies and measures. However, the path of health and healthcare development with Chinese characteristics must not waver," Xi said.

item.title: High-frequency data points to China's improving economic momentum in Q3
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
This photo taken with a mobile phone on Oct. 1, 2026 shows tourists at a local tea house in Haikou, south China's Hainan Province. (Xinhua/Guo Cheng)
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China's economy continued to improve in the third quarter of this year, with new growth drivers gaining momentum, official high-frequency data on consumption, trade and investment showed Sunday.
Consumer activity continued to recover, with offline consumption payments up 2.6 percent year on year in the third quarter, accelerating by 0.7 percentage points from the second quarter, according to data released by the State Information Center under the National Development and Reform Commission.
In September, offline consumption payments increased 3.1 percent from a year earlier, up 0.5 percentage points from August, marking three consecutive months of growth.
The data also showed that the weight carried by cargo ships departing from and arriving at major Chinese ports rose 43.1 percent and 0.3 percent year on year, respectively, in the third quarter.
On investment, the issuance of new special-purpose bonds rose 50.2 percent year on year in September, 43.6 percentage points faster than the August level, the data showed.
The value of contracts awarded for projects related to new infrastructure, including computing power, data and networks, increased 34.2 percent year on year in the third quarter and 50.4 percent year on year last month.
Capital investment in frontier sectors such as artificial intelligence and humanoid robots surged 184.1 percent year on year in the third quarter and 198.7 percent year on year in September, the data showed.
"Investment in frontier fields such as artificial intelligence has remained strong, supporting current growth while building momentum for the development of new quality productive forces," said Wei Ying, deputy director of the center's big data development department.
China has targeted 2026 growth at 4.5 to 5 percent and will strive for even better results in practice. In the first half of the year, the country's gross domestic product grew 4.7 percent year on year.
In another sign of a firming economy, China's manufacturing activity returned to expansionary territory in September, while non-manufacturing activity rebounded markedly. The purchasing managers' index for China's manufacturing sector stood at 50.1 last month, while the business activity index for the non-manufacturing sector reached 50.2.

item.title: Zheng Qinwen claims maiden WTA 1000 title at China Open
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
Zheng Qinwen poses with the trophy during the awarding ceremony after the women's singles final between Zheng Qinwen of China and Mirra Andreeva of Russia at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Fei)
BEIJING, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- China's Zheng Qinwen captured the women's singles title at the 2026 China Open on Sunday, defeating fourth-seeded Russian Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 in the final to claim her maiden WTA 1000 crown before breaking down in tears during an emotional celebration on home soil.
"The feeling is incredible. Winning here in Beijing, in front of my home crowd, has always been one of my dreams," Zheng said after the match.
The victory also made Zheng the first Chinese player to win the singles title at the China Open.
"Today's match was extremely tough. Mirra is a great player, and she broke my serve right at the start," Zheng said. "I just had to take it one point at a time and keep telling myself to hang in there and never give up. After playing so many matches, I was physically and mentally exhausted. But playing in front of my home crowd gave me that extra strength to keep pushing through."
"I want to congratulate Mirra on her outstanding achievement at Roland Garros this year. I never had a chance to congratulate you in person, so I want to do that now. Congratulations on reaching the final this week as well. You are such a young and talented player, and congratulations to you and your team on everything you've achieved," she added.
Since winning Olympic gold at the Paris 2024 Games, a persistent right elbow injury has disrupted Zheng's career and required surgery in July 2025. Her ranking subsequently fell from a career-high No. 4 in 2024 to as low as No. 160 in mid-June 2026.
"I want to thank my team for supporting me throughout this journey. I've been through a very tough year, and I couldn't have done this without you. Last but not least, I want to thank all the sponsors, the referees, and all the staff who have worked so hard throughout the week. And thank you to all the fans for your incredible support. This title belongs to all of you, too!"
The victory earned Zheng 1,000 ranking points and 1,151,380 U.S. dollars in prize money, lifting her to No. 23 in the live WTA rankings.
Zheng Qinwen (5th R, front) poses with the ballboys and ballgirls during the awarding ceremony after the women's singles final between Zheng Qinwen of China and Mirra Andreeva of Russia at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Fei)
Zheng Qinwen (R) and Mirra Andreeva pose with their trophies during the awarding ceremony after the women's singles final between Zheng Qinwen of China and Mirra Andreeva of Russia at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Fei)

item.title: Long March legacy inspires innovation breakthroughs in city of historic turning point
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12
*The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. The spirit of what American journalist Edgar Snow described as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times" continues to inspire China as it pursues its Second Centenary Goal.
*The Long March in Guizhou was about breaking through encirclement and relying on one's own strength. Today, we are far removed from the smoke of war, but in science and technology, we are also making breakthroughs.
*China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in the first half of this year, sets out comprehensive arrangements for accelerating high-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology and fostering new quality productive forces.
People visit the Zunyi Meeting memorial hall in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Zhengju/Xinhua)
ZUNYI, Guizhou, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Lei Guangren has crossed the weathered stone arch bridge countless times in Zunyi, a city in southwest China's Guizhou Province. Known as Yinghong Bridge, or "Welcoming the Red Army Bridge," it bears quiet witness to the Chinese Red Army's epic Long March more than nine decades ago.
Such Long March-associated place names pepper every corner of the mountainous city, earning Zunyi its resonant title: the "city of historic turning point."
"The Zunyi Meeting, held here during the Long March, marked a life-or-death turning point in the history of the Communist Party of China (CPC)," said Lei, 78, former curator of the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum. "From then on, the Party found the right direction and leadership, stayed the course toward its goals, defeated the enemies and embarked on a path of independence and self-reliance."
The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. Lei believes the spirit of what American journalist Edgar Snow described as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times" continues to inspire China as it pursues its Second Centenary Goal.
In October 1934, the CPC was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi Province and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party (KMT). The CPC-led Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the KMT troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle.
In downtown Zunyi stands a two-story gray-and-white building where Lei had worked for a decade. In January 1935, at a critical historical crossroads, the Zunyi Meeting was held in this building, establishing Mao Zedong's leading position in the CPC Central Committee and the Red Army in practice. The spirit of the Zunyi Meeting -- characterized by firm conviction, commitment to truth, independence and self-reliance, and unity -- continues to resonate today.
In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury wrote that China's course "had been set for at least half a century to come."
Tourists visit the historical site of the Zunyi Meeting in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Tian Jinhong/Xinhua)
The Red Army subsequently won its first major victory since the start of the Long March at Loushan Pass in northern Zunyi and later broke out of enemy encirclement through its four crossings of the Chishui River.
"My mother told me that she was working when Red Army soldiers passed by our home. They borrowed a douqiang to shelter from the rain," Lei recalled.
A douqiang is a bamboo-woven tool traditionally used in southern China for drying grain. By the time the rain stopped, the soldiers had already reached the neighboring village. Before leaving, however, they asked local residents to make sure the tool was returned to Lei's mother.
Salisbury's book also mentions Kong Xianquan, a Red Army soldier who led troops in an assault during the Battle of Loushan Pass. Hit by six bullets in the hip, Kong was left behind in Guizhou to recover from his wounds. After the founding of the People's Republic of China, he helped establish the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum and became its first curator.
Today, his granddaughter Kong Xia has spent more than three decades sharing stories of China's revolutionary history.
"In Zunyi, stories of the Red Army are passed down like family heirlooms, reminding each new generation not to forget where we came from or where we are going," she said.
For 56-year-old Kong, Zunyi is a city where tradition and modernity coexist. Xiaolongshan, where some Red Army martyrs were buried, was renamed Hongjunshan, or Red Army Mountain. Year after year, visitors come to pay tribute here beside a bronze statue of a Red Army soldier draped in red silk by local residents.
Beyond these landmarks, a 10-minute walk from the site of the Zunyi Meeting stands the theater for "The Great Turning Point," a large-scale immersive production about the Long March, where history is retold through live performance.
Chen Jinghong, a visitor from southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, brought her 10-year-old daughter to see the show. "It is like planting a seed in a child's heart, allowing her to experience the culture of the Long March and gradually understand and appreciate it as she grows up," Chen said.
But Zunyi is far more than a museum of revolution. It has undergone dramatic transformation. When the Red Army passed through, its population stood at just over 30,000. By 2025, the permanent population of its central urban area exceeded 1.6 million, with an urbanization rate of 61 percent.
An aerial drone photo taken on July 31, 2026 shows the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua)
And it is not just Zunyi that has developed. Guizhou, a mountainous province with no natural plains, has emerged as a "museum of bridges." Nearly half of the world's tallest bridges stand here.
"The Long March in Guizhou was about breaking through encirclement and relying on one's own strength," Kong said. "Today, we are far removed from the smoke of war, but in science and technology, we are also making breakthroughs."
One striking example is the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in Guizhou. Holding world records both as the highest and the longest-span steel truss girder suspension bridge located in mountainous terrain, it has been dubbed by Chinese internet users a bridge that is "world No. 1, both horizontally and vertically."
Its main cables and upper structural components were produced by Guizhou Wire Rope Co., Ltd. The core steel wires were both developed and manufactured in Guizhou, forming a critical lifeline for the project.
"Wire-rope production used to be dominated in many areas by European and American companies. After the efforts of several generations, our products are now widely used in major equipment across land, sea and air, helping overcome technological bottlenecks," said Yang Zhengyan, director of a product research and development office at Guizhou Wire Rope.
At Laoyashan, where fierce fighting involving the Red Army once took place, bullet marks can still be seen on the rocks. At the foot of the mountain lies the old factory compound of Guizhou Wire Rope.
It was there that Yang and his team conducted countless tests to develop a mooring cable for offshore engineering.
Such cables had previously been expensive and required long procurement cycles, posing constraints on the development of China's offshore oil and gas resources.
"There is no room for failure with a product like this, so for many tests that would normally have been conducted only once, we ran them over and over again. We also pioneered some testing methods," Yang said.
In August 2023, the first permanent mooring cable for a floating production, storage and offloading unit, or FPSO, developed by Guizhou Wire Rope, was successfully deployed in the mooring system of the "Nanhai Fenjin" FPSO. It marked China's first application of a domestically produced permanent mooring cable for an FPSO, ending the country's long-standing reliance on foreign products in this field.
The group is now capable of mass-producing the cable. It can be used not only for deep-sea oil production platforms, but also for offshore wind power platforms. The system can reduce the sea area occupied by conventional mooring systems to about one-tenth, while also reducing their environmental footprint.
"The spirit of the Long March tells me to find the right direction, not to act blindly, and not to fear hardship or failure," said Yang, a 46-year-old Guizhou native.
This photo taken on Aug. 17, 2026 shows a view of Loushan Pass in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua/Shi Qiangui)
For another Zunyi native, 52-year-old Lin Guojun, chairman of Shenzhen Busbar Sci-Tech Development Co., Ltd., the city has also played an important role in his company's growth.
Busbar holds more than 580 patents and international certifications, with its products used in new energy vehicles, wind power, solar power, smart grids and other new energy industries.
"We began developing our new energy business in 2008. It was an attempt to overtake on a curve," Lin recalled. "Back then, we had neither a market nor the technology, and the world did not believe China could develop a new energy industry."
In 2012, when the company encountered difficulties and struggled to fulfill orders, Lin turned his attention to Zunyi.
"Some of our equipment would shut down when temperatures became too high. Zunyi has a favorable natural environment, supporting industries, access to many major surrounding cities, and supportive policies," said Liu Yong, production and operations manager of Zunyi Busbar Sci-Tech Development Co., Ltd.
A new factory was completed in just seven months. Inside the plant, many production processes are semi-automated, with more than 40 robots and robotic arms operating in an orderly fashion to ensure greater consistency in product quality.
The Zunyi facility now focuses on developing and manufacturing high-voltage system components for new energy vehicles, including charging connectors, charging piles, high-voltage relays and high-voltage wiring harnesses. Its products are supplied directly to domestic and overseas automakers.
Lin, who grew up listening to stories about the Red Army, said he sees parallels between the Long March and his own industry.
"From a time when China's new energy sector was little known globally to today, when Chinese new energy vehicles have won worldwide recognition, our work in this industry has itself been a breakthrough," he said. "It takes perseverance and conviction to see something like this through."
Tourists experience VR devices at the Zunyi Meeting memorial hall in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Yuan Fuhong/Xinhua)
China's 15th Five-Year Plan, released in the first half of this year, sets out comprehensive arrangements for accelerating high-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology and fostering new quality productive forces. Among its seven major economic and social development goals for 2026-2030 is substantially boosting the country's capacity for independent innovation.
Zunyi's government work report this year also called for developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions and accelerating the building of a modern industrial system.
The national vision also plays out in ordinary people's lives. Kong is thinking of replacing her family's gasoline car with a new energy vehicle. A frequent traveler across China, she recently took a high-speed train to Yan'an. The trip, which once took the Red Army nine months, now takes less than nine hours.
Her 27-year-old son Jiang Xiao carries the legacy forward as part of a youth lecture group, sharing stories of the Long March.
"Every generation has different experiences and its own interpretation of the Long March spirit," Kong said. "Yet the spirit never fades with time, and these stories deserve to be passed on."
